::: {.why}
It replaces a fixed-horizon return with the outcome of an actual position with a stop and a target, which makes the label match the thing you would have experienced.
:::

## What you should be able to do tonight

- Implement triple-barrier labelling with barriers set from a volatility estimate rather than from fixed percentages.
- Report the label distribution and say what it tells you about the barrier widths you chose.

## Tasks <span class='task-total'>60 min</span>

::: {.task-list}
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [35 min]{.task-min} Implement it in qlib/ml/labels.py: for each observation, walk forward until the price crosses an upper barrier, a lower barrier, or the time limit, and record which. Set the barriers as multiples of the forecast volatility so they scale with the regime rather than being fixed percentages.
:::
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [25 min]{.task-min} Check the labels before modelling on them: report the fraction hitting each barrier. If almost everything hits the time limit the barriers are too wide to matter, and if almost nothing does they are too tight and you are labelling noise. Tune the multiples so all three outcomes are populated, and log that this tuning is itself a specification choice.
:::
:::

## The running strategy

::: {.project}
qlib/ml/labels.py implements volatility-scaled triple-barrier labelling with the outcome distribution reported, so the label reflects what a position with a stop and a target would have experienced.
:::
